Klaus Fuchs was a German-born British physicist who worked on the Manhattan Project and transmitted atomic bomb secrets to the Soviet Union during World War II. His exposure in nineteen fifty triggered the FBI's investigation that led to the arrests of Julius and Ethel Rosenberg, making him the catalyst for Cold War espionage investigations.

Fuchs fled Nazi Germany as a Communist sympathizer in nineteen thirty-three and worked as a theoretical physicist in Britain before being recruited by British intelligence to work on the American atomic bomb project. In nineteen forty-one, while working in Britain, he was recruited by Soviet intelligence and continued spying after joining the Manhattan Project at Los Alamos. He provided detailed technical information about bomb design and uranium enrichment.

Fuchs transmitted hand-written notes and technical sketches to his Soviet handler, giving Moscow access to the most advanced scientific secrets of the war. His information accelerated Soviet atomic development by years. In nineteen fifty, after the FBI began investigating Soviet penetration of the atomic program, Fuchs confessed to his espionage. His cooperation led directly to the identification and arrest of Julius Rosenberg and others.

Imprisoned in Britain for nine years, Fuchs was released in nineteen fifty-nine and moved to East Germany, where he worked as a physicist for the communist state until his death in nineteen eighty-eight. His exposure became a turning point in Cold War espionage, initiating investigations that would eventually uncover moles like Aldrich Ames decades later.
